documents.unit: UAF Center for Teaching and Learning
documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
documents.stance_why: The page is faculty guidance that sets no default for AI use; instead it says "Whatever your course policy is" and urges instructors to clarify expectations in the syllabus, so the decision is delegated to instructors.
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance for UAF instructors on generative AI: set and state your own syllabus expectations, teach citation, discuss plagiarism and AI errors, and consider AI uses for students and faculty. It notes detectors are unreliable and lists privacy and bias shortcomings.

units.why: The page tells instructors to "Clarify your expectations for the use of generative AI up front in your syllabus", an instruction to state AI expectations in the syllabus; instructor actor, course-start phase, should because it is advice ("Clarify"), and P09 fits as the syllabus-statement type.
units.anchor: Clarify your expectations for the use of generative AI up front in your syllabus.

units.why: "Whatever your course policy is" leaves the AI rule to each instructor, so the page itself sets no default; this is a delegation statement, so P04 (instructor sets the rule), not a stance type. It addresses instructors and is stated in the course-policy context.
units.anchor: Whatever your course policy is
units.policy: The course's AI policy is whatever the instructor sets.

units.why: "instruct students on how they should cite ChatGPT and other generative AI tools" tells instructors to teach citation of AI, so it is about disclosure/citation (P24); it is directed at instructors, at course start, as advice.
units.anchor: instruct students on how they should cite ChatGPT and other generative AI tools
units.policy: Instructors instruct students on how they should cite ChatGPT and other generative AI tools in their work.
units.fit_note: Concerns instructors teaching students how to cite; it does not itself require a citation.

units.why: "clarify the protocol you will follow should a student deliberately misuse the tool" asks instructors to state their misuse response in advance; closest is P37 (penalties stated in advance) but no penalty is named, so I note the partial fit rather than P36 which classifies misuse.
units.anchor: clarify the protocol you will follow should a student deliberately misuse the tool
units.policy: Instructors clarify the protocol they will follow should a student deliberately misuse the tool for classwork.
units.fit_note: Asks for a stated misuse protocol, not specific penalties.

units.why: The sentence points to "our institution’s Academic Misconduct Policy" as the governing process, which treats misuse as academic misconduct handled by integrity processes (P36); it informs rather than binds.
units.anchor: information on our institution’s Academic Misconduct Policy
units.policy: Information on the institution's Academic Misconduct Policy is available from the UAF Office of Rights, Compliance and Accountability.
units.fit_note: A pointer to the misconduct policy; it does not itself state that AI misuse is misconduct.

units.why: "The biggest concern is plagiarism" gives the reason behind AI rules, namely academic honesty; P95 (ground AI limits in academic honesty) fits better than P41 because no skill-building claim is made.
units.anchor: The biggest concern is plagiarism.

units.why: "Explain to students what constitutes plagiarism" asks instructors to give students the reasoning behind integrity rules, which is P66 (explain and discuss the rules) rather than P09 since it is about explanation, not listing a rule.
units.anchor: Explain to students what constitutes plagiarism
units.policy: Instructors explain to students what constitutes plagiarism and how that impacts the academic integrity of their work.

units.why: After the calculator analogy, "explain the difference between plagiarizing with AI and using it as an effective assistant" tells instructors to explain the line to students; P66 (explain and discuss), not P45 because the analogy is to a calculator tool, not a human collaborator.
units.anchor: explain the difference between plagiarizing with AI and using it as an effective assistant
units.policy: Instructors use the calculator example to explain the difference between plagiarizing with AI and using it as an effective assistant.

units.why: "an important discussion to have early in the semester with students" recommends timing and class discussion of AI use, so P66 with course-start phase and should modality.
units.anchor: This is an important discussion to have early in the semester with students.

units.why: The comparison to a "phone calculator" frames AI writing help as ordinary tool use; it is a rationale (informs) that normalizes AI assistance. P87 (benefits) is closer than P45 since no collaborator is invoked.
units.anchor: Using AI as a writing assistant may become as commonplace as using your phone calculator
units.policy: Using AI as a writing assistant may become as commonplace as using a phone calculator to do basic arithmetic.
units.fit_note: An analogy normalizing AI use, not a stated benefit.

units.why: The passage says training data "infringes on copyright and is used without consent", an intellectual-property concern about AI; P52 (copyright and licensing of AI) fits and it is informational.
units.anchor: contain some content that infringes on copyright and is used without consent
units.fit_note: Concerns copyright of training data rather than of inputs or outputs.

units.why: "replicate the stereotypes and biases" names a bias harm of AI, which is P53.
units.anchor: Generative AIs replicate the stereotypes and biases contained in the large language modules

units.why: "do not always comply with FERPA and HIPPA policies" is a privacy-law warning about AI tools; P50 (protect personal data, prefer vetted tools) is the nearest, stated as information.
units.anchor: Generative AIs do not always comply with FERPA and HIPPA policies.
units.fit_note: Warns of non-compliance but does not tell anyone to protect data.

units.why: "do not enable users the option to opt-out of having their own work used to train the model" is a data and privacy warning, P50, information only. Honorlock is named as an example in the next sentence.
units.anchor: some systems do not enable users the option to opt-out of having their own work

units.why: "Discuss how generative AI can return incorrect information and can even 'hallucinate'" tells instructors to discuss AI errors with students; P31 (AI output is often wrong) is the type, with a note that the directive is to instructors.
units.anchor: Discuss how generative AI can return incorrect information
units.policy: Instructors discuss with students how generative AI can return incorrect information and can even "hallucinate" false information.
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors to teach about errors, not to students to verify.

units.why: "demonstrates the importance of fact-checking generated results" states that AI output must be fact-checked, so P31; informs because it is framed as a lesson for instructors to show.
units.anchor: demonstrates the importance of fact-checking generated results

units.why: "Students can benefit from learning to use generative AI in many aspects of their lives" names a benefit of AI use without a rule; P87 (benefits) rather than P44 since careers are not mentioned here.
units.anchor: Students can benefit from learning to use generative AI in many aspects of their lives

units.why: "polishing language" lists AI polishing of writing as a possible student use, i.e. editing support, P91. It appears in a list of ideas, so modality is may and the stance permit.
units.anchor: polishing language
units.policy: Students might use generative AI in class for polishing language.

units.why: "generating ideas for article titles" is idea generation, P15. It appears in a list of ideas, so modality is may and the stance permit.
units.anchor: generating ideas for article titles
units.policy: Students might use generative AI in class for generating ideas for article titles.

units.why: "manipulating spreadsheets and data" is AI for data work, P89. It appears in a list of ideas, so modality is may and the stance permit.
units.anchor: manipulating spreadsheets and data
units.policy: Students might use generative AI in class for manipulating spreadsheets and data.

units.why: "solving equations" is listed as a possible student use of AI; it is solving problems, which fits no listed permitted use cleanly (not tutoring, debugging or code), so UNCOVERED. It appears in a list of ideas, so modality is may and the stance permit.
units.anchor: solving equations
units.policy: Students might use generative AI in class for solving equations.
units.uncovered_note: The page lists AI for solving equations as a possible student use.

units.why: "identifying blindspots in their thinking" is using AI to probe one's own reasoning, nearest to exploring approaches, P15. It appears in a list of ideas, so modality is may and the stance permit.
units.anchor: identifying blindspots in their thinking
units.policy: Students might use generative AI in class for identifying blindspots in their thinking.

units.why: "discovering opposing points of view" is using AI to explore alternative perspectives, P15. It appears in a list of ideas, so modality is may and the stance permit.
units.anchor: discovering opposing points of view
units.policy: Students might use generative AI in class for discovering opposing points of view.

units.why: "Revisiting the learning outcomes in your course may help you determine if and how generative AI is appropriate" ties the AI decision to learning outcomes (P83), and leaves the decision to the instructor.
units.anchor: Revisiting the learning outcomes in your course may help you determine if and how
units.policy: Instructors revisit course learning outcomes to determine if and how generative AI is appropriate for students.

units.why: "Communicate your expectations with your students" repeats the call to make writing expectations explicit; it follows a different question (polished work versus unique voice), so it is kept as a separate unit under P09.
units.anchor: Communicate your expectations with your students.
units.fit_note: Refers to expectations for student writing generally, not only AI.

units.why: "using generative AI for proofreading and editing allows students to focus on the content" supports permitting AI proofreading where writing is not a learning outcome; P91, stance permit, may modality, conditional on learning outcomes.
units.anchor: using generative AI for proofreading and editing allows students to focus on the content
units.policy: In classes where writing is not intrinsically linked to the learning outcomes, using generative AI for proofreading and editing allows students to focus on the content and less on the mechanics of writing.

units.why: "an assistive technology that helps reduce the anxiety of students for which English is a second language" presents AI as an accessibility aid, P97.
units.anchor: generative AI can also be considered an assistive technology that helps reduce the anxiety

units.why: "The UAF library has a resource that introduces generative AI" points students to an AI-literacy guide, P70.
units.anchor: The UAF library has a resource that introduces generative AI

units.why: "generative AI can also be a tool in your arsenal" affirms that instructors may use AI in teaching, introducing the list below; P59 (instructor use for teaching work).
units.anchor: If you are teaching, generative AI can also be a tool in your arsenal.

units.why: "Iterate on a syllabus" suggests instructors use ChatGPT to draft a syllabus, with instructor edits afterward; P59.
units.anchor: Iterate on a syllabus
units.policy: Instructors may use generative AI to iterate on a syllabus, editing its recommendations based on their expertise.

units.why: "Rethink assignment design" asks whether students need mechanics of writing and whether AI can be allowed "as an editor or collaborator"; this redesigns assignments around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Rethink assignment design
units.policy: Instructors rethink assignment design, considering allowing generative AI in as an editor or collaborator where mastering the mechanics of writing is not needed for the course outcomes.

units.why: "involving them in the decision to use chatGPT for particular assignments" has instructors set AI use together with students, P67.
units.anchor: involving them in the decision to use chatGPT for particular assignments
units.policy: Instructors involve students in the decision to use ChatGPT for particular assignments.

units.why: "ask ChatGPT to create one" suggests instructors have AI generate an example assignment artifact; P59.
units.anchor: ask ChatGPT to create one
units.policy: Instructors may ask ChatGPT to create an example of a completed assignment to show students.

units.why: "Show students how to leverage generative AI as a teaching assistant" for "code syntax or formatting" questions endorses AI help with syntax; P13 (explain errors, clarify syntax) is the nearest.
units.anchor: Show students how to leverage generative AI as a teaching assistant
units.policy: Instructors show students how to leverage generative AI as a teaching assistant for questions about code syntax or formatting.
units.fit_note: Framed as offloading instructor workload; the permission to students is implied.

units.why: "Students may benefit from a CliffsNotes style summary" proposes AI-made lesson summaries for study, P14.
units.anchor: Students may benefit from a CliffsNotes style summary of content that you have already provided

units.why: "foster the development of AI-literacy skills" states the center's aim of teaching AI use and improving learning; P44 (teach effective AI use) chosen over P87 since the sentence is about AI literacy goals.
units.anchor: foster the development of AI-literacy skills

units.why: "Join us for upcoming workshops" invites faculty to workshops on AI in teaching, P63.
units.anchor: Join us for upcoming workshops to explore and share ideas.

units.why: The page recommends an AlaskaX course, "Teaching and Learning in the Era of AI", as faculty learning, P63.
units.anchor: taking “Teaching and Learning in the Era of AI,” an edX course from AlaskaX

units.why: "There are no tools which can reliably detect AI-generated writing" says detectors are unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: There are no tools which can reliably detect AI-generated writing

units.why: "using other forms of assessment or embracing AI by modeling good behavior" recommends assessment redesign in response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: using other forms of assessment or embracing AI by modeling good behavior

units.why: "the incorporation of a revision cycle with reflection" is an assignment redesign for essays, P35.
units.anchor: the incorporation of a revision cycle with reflection
units.policy: Instructors can adapt the essay by incorporating a revision cycle with reflection.

units.why: "three AI-based tools which can help in generating learning materials and activities, and make grading and feedback easier for instructors" describes instructor use of AI for materials and feedback, P59 (informs).
units.anchor: three AI-based tools which can help in generating learning materials and activities
units.fit_note: Mentions tools that ease grading and feedback; conditions on AI grading are not given.

documents.unit: University of Alaska System Office of Information Technology (system-wide, applies to UAF)
documents.title: Generative AI Security Standard
documents.stance_why: The standard says the "University of Alaska supports responsible exploration with Generative AI tools" and then conditions it on data, attribution and legal compliance, with instructors to state classroom rules; it is permission with conditions, not a ban or a pure delegation.
documents.summary: A mandatory University of Alaska system information-security standard on generative AI. It defines terms, warns about data, IP, bias and accuracy risks, requires attribution and legal compliance, bans some uses, and defers classroom rules to instructors and academic-integrity policy.

units.why: "communicate expectations and requirements related to use of Generative AI throughout the UA System" states purpose and scope of an institution-wide framework, P56.
units.anchor: communicate expectations and requirements related to use of Generative AI throughout the UA System

units.why: "are mandatory and apply to the UA System and all users of UA computing resources" sets who the standard binds, a scope statement (P56).
units.anchor: are mandatory and apply to the UA System and all users of UA computing resources

units.why: Units "may add additional requirements" but "may not weaken any individual element", so units may set their own rules above a floor; P85 (units set own rules).
units.anchor: may add additional requirements or detail as appropriate for their business needs
units.frag_end: an approved Information Security Controls Exception
units.fit_note: Units may add requirements but not weaken the baseline.

units.why: "periodically reviewed and updated" commits to a review cycle, P54.
units.anchor: This standard is periodically reviewed and updated to respond to emerging threats

units.why: "reviewed and approved by the CIO Management Team (CMT)" says which body adopts the standard, P84.
units.anchor: reviewed and approved by the CIO Management Team (CMT)

units.why: The definition of "AI" sets what the standard covers, P61.
units.anchor: The term “AI” refers to computer systems that are capable of performing tasks traditionally

units.why: This defines "Generative AI (GenAI)", a scope definition, P61.
units.anchor: Services or applications that use deep learning models to create new content

units.why: "University of Alaska supports responsible exploration with Generative AI tools" sets a default of allowing AI with caution, P02 (permit by default); the risk list is conditions.
units.anchor: University of Alaska supports responsible exploration with Generative AI tools

units.why: "responsible for considering and mitigating risks related to the use of Generative AI" assigns users responsibility for risk; no listed type is about risk responsibility (P29 is about owning submitted work), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: are responsible for considering and mitigating risks related to the use of Generative AI
units.uncovered_note: Employees and students are responsible for considering and mitigating the risks of generative AI use.

units.why: "can potentially be stored on servers not controlled by the University of Alaska" warns about data exposure, P50.
units.anchor: can potentially be stored on servers not controlled by the University of Alaska

units.why: "must be handled in strict compliance with applicable privacy and data protection laws" requires legal compliance for data used with AI, P77 (comply with law).
units.anchor: must be handled in strict compliance with applicable privacy and data protection laws and regulations

units.why: The passage warns that "copyrighted, proprietary, research, educational, or non-public information" given to AI may be stored externally; an IP and data warning, P52 (informs) rather than P49 since it does not forbid uploads.
units.anchor: Any copyrighted, proprietary, research, educational, or non-public information provided to Generative AI
units.fit_note: Warns about exposure of IP; no rule is stated.

units.why: "biases that make existing inequalities worse" is a bias harm, P53.
units.anchor: biases that make existing inequalities worse

units.why: "commit to reducing it via Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) verification" tells developers and users to verify output to cut bias; nearest P31 (verify AI output).
units.anchor: commit to reducing it via Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) verification
units.policy: Developers and users of generative AI should be aware of bias risk and commit to reducing it via Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) verification.
units.fit_note: Verification is aimed at bias reduction, not only factual accuracy.

units.why: "it must be carefully reviewed and validated" requires checking AI output, P31.
units.anchor: it must be carefully reviewed and validated

units.why: "reviewed by at least one domain expert" before publishing AI results adds a human review step, P31 with a note that the reviewer is an expert.
units.anchor: should be reviewed by at least one domain expert
units.fit_note: Names a domain-expert reviewer before publication.

units.why: "may gather information about how users interact with it, sometimes without telling them" is a data privacy warning, P50.
units.anchor: may gather information about how users interact with it, sometimes without telling them

units.why: "must be securely stored and handled according to the UA’s data handling policies" requires data protection, P50.
units.anchor: must be securely stored and handled according to the UA’s data handling policies

units.why: "avoid using services that haven’t been approved" tells users to use approved tools only, P92 (should-not).
units.anchor: avoid using services that haven’t been approved for use by the University of Alaska

units.why: "Be cautious when clicking links, and make sure you have good antivirus protection" is security-awareness advice about AI outputs; P75.
units.anchor: Be cautious when clicking links, and make sure you have good antivirus protection.
units.fit_note: Concerns links in AI output and antivirus, not phishing explicitly.

units.why: "Don’t use it for illegal activities, to violate others' rights" bans unlawful use of AI, P74.
units.anchor: Don’t use it for illegal activities, to violate others' rights
units.fit_note: Also covers discussing sensitive topics that risk others' privacy.

units.why: "Avoid sharing information that is legally or confidentially restricted" tells users not to put restricted data into AI, P50 (should-not).
units.anchor: Avoid sharing information that is legally or confidentially restricted.

units.why: "read, understand, and follow the platform’s terms of service" is about terms of use of AI tools, P52 (should).
units.anchor: make sure to read, understand, and follow the platform’s terms of service

units.why: "a list of vetted Generative AI applications" points to approved tools, P92 (informs).
units.anchor: University of Alaska has a list of vetted Generative AI applications

units.why: "should follow responsible human-centered design architecture and deployment principles" gives a principle for AI use, a framework statement, P56.
units.anchor: AI use should follow responsible human-centered design architecture and deployment principles

units.why: "its use needs to be consistent with the University of Alaska Board of Regents' policies" requires AI use to follow existing policy and law, P77.
units.anchor: its use needs to be consistent with the University of Alaska Board of Regents' policies

units.why: "must adhere to UA's Data Classification Standards" requires deployments to follow data rules, P50.
units.anchor: Generative AI deployments must adhere to UA's Data Classification Standards
units.frag_end: adhere to UA's Data Classification Standards
units.fit_note: Addresses deployments and data classification, not personal data alone.

units.why: "must immediately stop using the technology and contact the OIT Information Security and Assurance Office" sets a duty to report breaches or risks, P71.
units.anchor: must immediately stop using the technology and contact the OIT Information Security and Assurance Office

units.why: "prohibited from using Generative AI to reverse engineer, decompile, and/or develop competing AI models" is a licensing-based ban, nearest P52 (terms of use).
units.anchor: are prohibited from using Generative AI to reverse engineer, decompile, and/or develop competing AI models
units.fit_note: A prohibition tied to licensing terms rather than ownership of outputs.

units.why: "must be requested and approved via the Information Security Controls Standard" sets the exception process, P80.
units.anchor: which must be requested and approved via the Information Security Controls Standard
units.frag_end: approved via the Information Security Controls Standard

units.why: "prohibited from using Generative AI to identify anonymized or pseudonymized human research subjects" bans re-identification, a data-privacy rule, P50 (must-not).
units.anchor: prohibited from using Generative AI to identify anonymized or pseudonymized human research subjects

units.why: "All work created using Generative AI must include proper attribution, including the AI system(s) used" requires disclosure, P24; P25 does not fit since prompts are not required.
units.anchor: All work created using Generative AI must include proper attribution
units.fit_note: Names the AI system used but not prompt or date.

units.why: "will use a human in-the-loop approach" requires human review of AI output; P31 is nearest, and P73 does not fit since decisions about individuals are not the subject.
units.anchor: will use a human in-the-loop approach to guard against Generative AI output
units.fit_note: Human-in-the-loop to guard against dangerous results and bias.

units.why: "monitoring and auditing outcomes" with "fairness safeguards" and transparency describes auditing of AI systems, P98.
units.anchor: implementing fairness safeguards, monitoring and auditing outcomes, and ensuring transparency

units.why: "Instructors should be clear with students on what, if any, and how Generative AI is allowed" asks instructors to state the AI rule in coursework and leaves it to them; P09 is chosen over P04 since the emphasis is communication.
units.anchor: monitoring and auditing outcomes, and ensuring transparency
units.fit_note: Also leaves whether AI is allowed to the instructor.

units.why: "Students are encouraged to ask their instructors for guidance or clarification" is P10.
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to ask their instructors for guidance or clarification if needed.

units.why: "Review and understand your university’s policies on academic integrity" tells students to learn the applicable rules, P78.
units.anchor: Review and understand your university’s policies on academic integrity

units.why: "may subject students to disciplinary action including expulsion" states possible penalties for violating security controls, P37; it applies to circumvention of security controls, not only academic misuse.
units.anchor: may subject students to disciplinary action including expulsion
units.fit_note: Penalties apply to circumventing information security controls.

units.why: "may subject employees to disciplinary action, up to and including termination" is the employee-side penalty, P37.
units.anchor: may subject employees to disciplinary action, up to and including termination
units.fit_note: Penalties apply to circumventing information security controls.

units.why: "responsible for the implementation, maintenance and interpretation" names who owns the standard, P80.
units.anchor: OIT Information Security and Assurance is responsible for the implementation, maintenance and interpretation

units.why: "Updated: March 2025 (included material from content-area experts)" says how the standard was made, P84.
units.anchor: Updated: March 2025 (included material from content-area experts)

units.why: "Next Review: January 2027" sets a dated review, P54.
units.anchor: Next Review: January 2027

documents.title: Using AI as a Student (eCampus Blackboard students page)
documents.stance_why: The post tells students the AI rule may "vary from course to course" and to learn it from the syllabus and the professor, while freeing AI as a study aid; the page sets no uniform rule, so it delegates to courses.
documents.summary: A 2023 student-facing blog post from UAF's Center for Teaching and Learning. It advises students to follow each course's AI rules, cite AI when paraphrasing, ask when unsure, and use ChatGPT for practice questions regardless of course policy.

units.why: "do not cheat" is advice from a CTL instructional designer, not a rule on AI as such; P95 (honesty) is nearest, with a fit note.
units.anchor: do not cheat
units.fit_note: General advice against cheating, not specific to AI.

units.why: The page cites the Student Code of Conduct, which lists "Cheating, Plagiarism, or Other Forms of Academic Dishonesty" as "prohibited"; it connects AI misuse to the misconduct code, P36.
units.anchor: Cheating, Plagiarism, or Other Forms of Academic Dishonesty
units.fit_note: Quotes the general code; AI is not named.

units.why: "pay attention to are the particulars for each of your courses" tells students to learn each course's AI rules, P78.
units.anchor: What you need to pay attention to are the particulars for each of your courses.

units.why: "vary from course to course" says AI-related permissions differ by course, P11 (a course's policy governs only that course).
units.anchor: One thing that might very well vary from course to course

units.why: "allowed to paraphrase results you get back from some of the text-generating AIs" says paraphrasing AI output may be allowed (in some courses); P18 for prose use.
units.anchor: allowed to paraphrase results you get back from some of the text-generating AIs
units.policy: Students may be allowed to paraphrase results they get back from some text-generating AIs, depending on the course.
units.fit_note: Permission is course-dependent.

units.why: "some faculty that prohibit AIs as sources, some that allow it, and others that encourage it" describes instructor-level variation, P04.
units.anchor: some faculty that prohibit AIs as sources, some that allow it

units.why: "you will need to make the correct citation" requires citing AI when paraphrased, P24.
units.anchor: you will need to make the correct citation

units.why: "reading the syllabus and asking your professor" tells students where to find the rule, P78.
units.anchor: you’ll know what to expect in a course from reading the syllabus

units.why: "If you are ever in doubt ... just ask!" is P10.
units.anchor: If you are ever in doubt about an assignment’s details or the policies

units.why: "perfectly free to do, whether or not your professor allows AI use ... leveraging AIs as a study aid" permits AI for study regardless of course policy, P14.
units.anchor: is leveraging AIs as a study aid
units.policy: Students are perfectly free to leverage AIs as a study aid, whether or not their professor allows AI use in course assignments.
units.fit_note: Also states the permission holds regardless of the course's AI policy.

units.why: "Consider asking ChatGPT to generate various practice questions" recommends practice problems, P14.
units.anchor: Consider asking ChatGPT to generate various practice questions:

units.why: "edit your question (engineer your prompt)" is practical prompting advice, P93.
units.anchor: just edit your question (engineer your prompt)

units.why: "go through multiple rounds of this process" advises iterating prompts, P93.
units.anchor: Don’t be afraid to go through multiple rounds of this process

units.why: "start to fail when you get more and more specific" warns of AI accuracy limits, P31; informs, no verification instruction.
units.anchor: start to fail when you get more and more specific
units.fit_note: Describes limits; it does not instruct to verify.

units.why: "more than welcome to visit the MIX space" gives access to paid ChatGPT on campus, nearest P51 (free access provided).
units.anchor: more than welcome to visit the MIX space at UAF’s Center for Teaching
units.fit_note: Offers on-site use of a paid version; no statement about cost barriers.

notes: Coder B. Course layer deferred in collect file. Several UA standard units (risk responsibility, human-in-the-loop) are close calls between UNCOVERED and P31/P56; fit_notes record the gaps.
